paragraphs.title: Remembering God's Deeds in the Past

easy.explanation: The psalm says, “our fathers have told us.”
easy.q: Who told the people about God's works in ancient times?

easy.explanation: The passage says that God drove out the heathen and planted His people.
easy.q: Who drove out the heathen and planted Israel?

easy.explanation: The people did not possess the land by their own sword or arm.
easy.q: What did not give Israel the land?

medium.explanation: The fathers' testimony reminds the people of what God did in ancient times.
medium.q: What is the purpose of remembering the fathers' testimony?

medium.explanation: God cast the nations out by removing them from the land.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “cast them out” mean?

answers: God's right hand, arm, and favor
medium.explanation: The psalm credits God's power and favor rather than human strength.
medium.q: What is presented as the reason for Israel's success?

challenge.explanation: Israel did not gain the land by its own sword, but through God's power.
challenge.q: What contrast is emphasized in these verses?

answers: It is based on remembered testimony of God's past acts
It rejects everything from the past
It depends only on military strength
challenge.explanation: The people look back to the ancient testimony of God's works.
challenge.q: What does “in the times of old” suggest about the people's faith?

challenge.explanation: The phrase is joined with God's right hand, arm, and favor toward His people.
challenge.q: What does God's “light of thy countenance” communicate in context?

paragraphs.title: A Plea for Salvation and Trust in God

easy.explanation: The verse begins, “Thou art my King, O God.”
easy.q: How does the people address God?

easy.explanation: The people ask God to “command deliverances for Jacob.”
easy.q: For whom does the people ask deliverance?

easy.explanation: The people say, “through thy name will we tread them under.”
easy.q: In whose name will the people tread down their enemies?

answers: A request for God to bring salvation
A command for Jacob to surrender
A wish for the enemy to rule
medium.explanation: The people ask their King to order or bring deliverance.
medium.q: What does “command deliverances for Jacob” express?

medium.explanation: The expression describes victory over those who rise against God's people.
medium.q: What does “push down our enemies” mean in context?

answers: Because God is their true source of salvation
Because bows are forbidden in the passage
medium.explanation: The psalm says, “I will not trust in my bow,” and declares that God saves them.
medium.q: Why will the people not trust in their bow?

answers: The people appeal to the ruler who has authority to save them
The people ask the enemy to become king
challenge.explanation: As King, God is the rightful one to whom the people turn for salvation.
challenge.q: What is the connection between calling God “my King” and asking for deliverance?

answers: Victory comes through God, not weapons
challenge.explanation: The people push down enemies through God and do not trust in bow or sword.
challenge.q: What repeated idea appears in verses 5–7?

answers: It declares trust in God and then says, “In God we boast”
It abandons faith and becomes silent
challenge.explanation: The people trust God's saving power and praise His name continually.
challenge.q: How does the passage move from confidence to praise?

paragraphs.title: Rejection, Defeat, and Humiliation in the Present

easy.explanation: The people complain that God “goest not forth with our armies.”
easy.q: What does the people say God no longer does with their armies?

easy.explanation: The enemies take their possessions for themselves.
easy.q: What do those who hate the people do?

easy.explanation: The passage says God scattered them “among the heathen.”
easy.q: Among whom has the people been scattered?

answers: They feel that God does not go forth with their armies
They have already conquered the enemy
They want to move to another land
medium.explanation: Their retreat is described alongside the complaint that God does not go with them.
medium.q: What causes the people to turn back from the enemy?

medium.explanation: The enemies take the people's possessions as plunder.
medium.q: What does “spoil” mean in “they which hate us spoil for themselves”?

answers: As a reproach, scorn, and derision
medium.explanation: The passage uses several words describing disgrace and mockery.
medium.q: How are the people treated by those around them?

answers: Earlier God gave victory; now the people experience defeat and disgrace
Earlier the people were scattered; now they are mocked
Earlier there were no enemies; now there is peace
challenge.explanation: The past was marked by God's victory, while the present is marked by retreat, loss, and shame.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast between the earlier verses and this section?

answers: The depth of the people's public humiliation
challenge.explanation: The accumulation of terms stresses how openly the people are mocked.
challenge.q: What does the repeated language of reproach, scorn, derision, and a byword emphasize?

answers: The shame is ongoing and constantly visible
The shame lasted only one moment
The people have forgotten their trouble
challenge.explanation: “Continually” shows that the confusion remains before them without relief.
challenge.q: What does “my confusion is continually before me” add to the description?

easy.explanation: The people say, “yet have we not forgotten thee.”
easy.q: What does the people say they have not forgotten?

answers: They have dealt falsely in it
They have not dealt falsely in it
They have never heard of it
easy.explanation: The verse says, “neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant.”
easy.q: What does the people say about God's covenant?

easy.explanation: The people say, “we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.”
easy.q: What are the people counted as?

answers: They suffer despite saying they have not forgotten God or broken His covenant
They admit that they abandoned God
They say their suffering is imaginary
medium.explanation: The people insist that their suffering is not the result of forgetting God or turning from Him.
medium.q: What is the relationship between the people's suffering and their claim of faithfulness?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the inner things known by God.
medium.q: What are “the secrets of the heart”?

answers: God knows whether their faithfulness is genuine
God is unaware of their motives
They want the enemy to judge them
medium.explanation: Because God searches the heart, He knows the truth about their loyalty.
medium.q: Why does the people appeal to God's knowledge of the heart?

answers: The people suffer while claiming continued loyalty to God
The people are trying to forget God's name
challenge.explanation: The verse places their continual suffering alongside their devotion to God.
challenge.q: What does “for thy sake are we killed all the day long” communicate?

answers: Faithfulness to the covenant includes inward loyalty, not merely outward actions
The heart represents complete rejection of God
challenge.explanation: The people say their heart has not turned back, and God knows the heart's secrets.
challenge.q: How are the heart and the covenant connected in this section?

answers: The disasters and suffering described before the claim of faithfulness
challenge.explanation: “All this” summarizes the troubles that have come upon the people.
challenge.q: What does “All this” refer to in verse 18?

paragraphs.title: A Cry for Awakening and Redemption

easy.explanation: The people call to the Lord, saying, “Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord?”
easy.q: To whom are the words “Awake” and “arise” addressed?

easy.explanation: They ask why God forgets their affliction and oppression.
easy.q: What does the people ask God not to forget?

easy.explanation: The final request is, “Arise for our help, and redeem us.”
easy.q: What does the people ask God to do at the end?

answers: Their soul is bowed to the dust and their belly cleaves to the earth
They have already won the battle
medium.explanation: These images describe their extreme humiliation and distress.
medium.q: Why does the people cry out for God's help?

medium.explanation: The people ask God to deliver them from their desperate condition.
medium.q: What does “redeem us” mean in this context?

answers: They ask God not to abandon them and appeal to His mercy
They declare that God has abandoned them forever
They rely only on their own strength
medium.explanation: The prayer seeks deliverance on the basis of God's mercies.
medium.q: What is the relationship between “cast us not off for ever” and “for thy mercies' sake”?

answers: The people move from describing their pain to directly asking God to act
The people announce the enemy's victory
challenge.explanation: The prayer progresses from lament to an urgent appeal for divine action.
challenge.q: What change occurs from the questions “Why?” to the command “Arise”?

challenge.explanation: Both expressions picture the people as crushed and brought very low.
challenge.q: What do “bowed down to the dust” and “cleaveth unto the earth” communicate?

answers: Because the requested redemption depends on God's compassion
Because the people claim their own power is sufficient
Because the enemies have already disappeared
challenge.explanation: The people ask to be redeemed “for thy mercies' sake,” relying on God's kindness.
challenge.q: Why does the final appeal rest on God's mercies rather than the people's strength?
